name: Decree-law 2022-68 (19 Oct 2022): faster public and private projects, with renewables allowed on farmland without a change of use
owner: Presidency of the Republic (decree-law); applied by the Ministries of Industry/Energy, Agriculture and Equipment, and the Tunisian Investment Authority

claims.claim: Art. 21 adds art. 5 bis to law 2015-12: renewable projects are built on private land, or on leased public (agricultural or non-agricultural) or local-authority land after a technical committee confirms feasibility; they do not require a change of use of agricultural land.
Art. 21 also lets the public body pay grid-connection and grid-reinforcement costs when the State proposes the site.

Art. 17 rewrites art. 8 ter of law 83-87: change of use of farmland for public projects and direct-investment operations (except projects falling under the Tunisian Investment Authority) is by joint arrêté of the agriculture and urbanism ministers on the regional commission's opinion, within three months; if the administration stays silent, the file goes to the Investment Authority's approvals commission.
The measures are meant to remove land-access and grid problems that slow renewable projects (as presented in a tier C press summary; the decree-law text itself states no such aim for art. 21).
The reform speeds up renewable roll-out.
Renewable projects on farmland harm farming and food security.

limits: Acts on land access and, for State-proposed sites, grid-connection cost. It does not touch the other documented causes of slow delivery: STEG as sole offtaker and its finances, the multi-step authorisation and parliament procedure, ageing grid (FND-TG-191).

Art. 5 bis sets no land-class limit, no 'degraded land first' rule, no area cap and no agrivoltaic or dual-use requirement. Whatever land safeguards exist come from elsewhere (art. 5 bis overrides only arts. 6 and 8 of law 83-87, the change-of-use rules; whether other provisions of that law still apply to renewables was not checked).

Because the land is not re-zoned, a plant on farmland would leave no change-of-use decree or commission file from which to count the area affected (inference from the text; no register was looked for beyond the sources opened).

blockers.blocker: Grid capacity and STEG finances remain the binding constraints on utility-scale plants; the 2022 text only shifts connection costs for State-proposed sites.
Public land under lease still has to pass the technical committee feasibility test and the military-domain legislation (art. 5 bis).
Agrivoltaics, the dual-use option, is at an early pilot stage: ANME plans demonstration projects, no site or result reported.

criticisms.criticism: Productive farmland should be protected when solar concessions are approved (opposition deputies, April 2026 debate on five concessions; also raised tariff transparency and arbitration clauses).
Farmers' unions, civil society and researchers: no criticism of art. 5 bis from a farmers' union, NGO or peer-reviewed paper was found in the sources opened.

tradeOffs.effect: Possible long-term loss of cropland or pasture to solar plants, with no register of area, land class or former use. Observed so far in one project only: Khobna, 267.74 ha of State land used for grazing and not cropped; the developer's own study says direct impacts concern farmland and pastureland. The wider loss is an argument and a risk, not an observation.

Because art. 5 bis says renewable projects do not require a change of use of farmland, notwithstanding arts. 6 and 8 of law 83-87, the change-of-use procedure of that law (regional commission opinion, ministerial decision) is not required for renewables.

The same decree-law (art. 17 and art. 28) sets a three-month deadline with an Investment Authority fallback for change of use for other investment projects and allows regularisation of industrial plants already built on farmland; this is a farmland effect of the decree-law as a whole, not of its renewables article.

gapLeft: Delivery speed is not shown to improve; the 2030 gap (FND-TG-192) rests mainly on offtaker finance, procedures and grid. No registry of land used by solar plants by class and former use; no siting rule that steers plants to degraded, State or non-productive land; dual use (agrivoltaics) is only a pilot.
author: TahaGHZ

sections.heading: What it is
sections.content:
Decree-law 2022-68 of 19 October 2022 contains "special provisions to improve the efficiency of public and private projects" (SRC-TG-202, gazette No. 114 of 21 October 2022). Three groups of articles matter here.

- **Art. 21: renewables.** It adds art. 5 bis and a second paragraph to art. 8 of law 2015-12 on electricity from renewables. Art. 5 bis: "Les projets de production des énergies renouvelables sont réalisés sur les terrains appartenant aux privés", with leased public agricultural and non-agricultural or local-authority land as an option after a feasibility check by the technical committee, subject to military-domain legislation. Then: "Nonobstant les dispositions des articles 6 et 8 de la loi n° 83-87 [...] la réalisation des projets de production de l'électricité des énergies renouvelables ne requiert pas le changement d'affectation des terres agricoles." Art. 8 para. 2: where the State proposes the site, the public body may bear grid-connection and reinforcement costs (SRC-TG-202; same reading in SRC-TG-370).
- **Art. 22.** Replaces art. 31 of law 2015-12: on State land the producer gets a special real right over buildings and equipment, not over the land (SRC-TG-202).
- **Art. 17 and 28: farmland and investment.** Art. 17 rewrites art. 8 ter of law 83-87. Change of use for public projects and direct-investment operations, except projects falling under the Tunisian Investment Authority, is by joint arrêté of the agriculture and urbanism ministers, on the regional commission's opinion, within three months, with a reasoned rejection within ten days. After silence, the file goes to the Investment Authority's approvals commission, with the authorisation granted after checking conditions and deadlines (art. 15 bis of law 2016-71) (SRC-TG-202). Art. 28 covers change of use, by joint arrêté, of farmland on which industrial projects were built before the decree-law; conditions (investment size, jobs, tax regularisation, environment) are set by a joint arrêté, and the Investment Authority lists the projects (SRC-TG-202; the 3 May 2023 arrêté criteria in SRC-TG-853, tier C).

Related texts not opened: law 2019-47 (first version of art. 8 ter), the industry arrêté of 3 May 2023, the 2022 and 2026 concession laws.

sections.heading: What it claims, and what the evidence shows
sections.content:
The decree-law's stated purpose is to speed up projects. For renewables, press summaries present art. 21 as solving "problèmes d'ordre foncier et de raccordement" (SRC-TG-370). The legal text is confirmed. No source opened measures its effect on delivery time or capacity built. FND-TG-191 records that no source quantifies how often land access blocked a project, and that delays rest on finance, procedure and grid as well. The record therefore treats art. 21 as a plausible fix for one cause.

Note on FND-TG-841: the gazette text of art. 8 ter (nouveau) says the change of use is by joint arrêté on commission opinion, and after silence the Investment Authority commission grants the authorisation after verification (SRC-TG-202). SRC-TG-853 says "accordée d'office" and says the minister's authorisation was replaced by the commission opinion alone. The gazette text does not use the word "d'office"; it says the authorisation is granted after verification of conditions and deadlines, so "d'office" is the summary's gloss. The gazette text also excludes projects falling under the Investment Authority from the arrêté route. Whether this explains the Mhamdia arrêté in FND-TG-841 was not checked.

sections.heading: Audit
sections.content:
**root_cause_coverage: 1.** FND-TG-191 lists five causes: STEG as sole offtaker and its finances, authorisation procedure, grid connection, land and local acceptance, and bidding and finance. Art. 21 acts on the land cause (no change of use needed) and part of the grid cause (State-proposed sites only). The FND-TG-192 gap rests mainly on the other causes. It acts on a real but secondary cause, hence 1.

**evidence_quality: 1.** The legal text is tier A and opened. There is no evaluation, statistic or independent study of the effect on delivery, and no study of land used. The criticism evidence is a press report of a debate (tier C).

**adoption: 2.** The text is in force. Projects on State sites are going ahead: the five concession bills approved in April 2026 (SRC-TG-372) and Khobna on State land (SRC-TG-371). Whether art. 5 bis was actually invoked for farmland, as opposed to State land used for grazing, is not shown.

**side_effects: 1.** Art. 21 removes the change-of-use step of law 83-87 (arts. 6 and 8) for renewables and the text adds no replacement rule: no class limit, no degraded-land-first rule, no area register, no dual-use requirement. The farmland effect of the same decree-law's arts. 17 and 28 adds to this. The one measured project (Khobna, 267.74 ha) was grazing land with no cropping (developer's statement, SRC-TG-371), so observed loss to cropland is not shown. Score 1 and not 0 because actual loss is unmeasured and the one documented site was not cropland.

**cost_accessibility: 2.** The legal change costs the State little. When the State proposes the site it may pay connection and grid-reinforcement costs (SRC-TG-202), which falls on STEG and the public budget (see FND-TG-161 for STEG's finances).

sections.heading: Limits and blockers
sections.content:
- Art. 5 bis (SRC-TG-202) is permissive and has no siting criteria. Nothing in it ranks degraded or State land ahead of fertile land; the preference for private land and leased public land is not a land-quality test.
- Grid and offtaker constraints are untouched (FND-TG-191). The 2022 text does not create a tariff or regulator change.
- Other legal blockers: the technical committee's feasibility test and the military-domain legislation for leased public land (SRC-TG-202). Decree 2016-1123 (art. 14) caps projects for local consumption that need a ministerial authorisation at 10 MW for PV; that decree is not amended by the text read here (SRC-TG-201).
- Agrivoltaics is not mandated. ANME has launched a call for demonstration projects after GIZ-funded strategic studies (SRC-TG-373, 2025); no pilot result was found.

sections.heading: Criticisms
sections.content:
- **Opposition deputies (2026).** When parliament approved five concessions (Khobna, Mazzouna, El Ksour, Sagdoud, Menzel El Habib) they asked for protection of productive farmland, along with tariff, arbitration and sovereignty objections (SRC-TG-372). Partly supported: the text has no safeguard to point to, but the report gives no hectares, and the one documented site (SRC-TG-371) was grazing land.
- **Farmers' unions, civil society, researchers.** None found in the sources opened. Search results also pointed to a Legal Agenda article and a Nawaat investigation on land grabbing in the south, a Climate Home News piece (Feb 2022) on Tozeur farmers, and a Business and Human Rights Resource Centre item on EU green-energy deals. The Legal Agenda and BHRRC pages could not be opened (HTTP 403), the Climate Home page was paywalled, and Nawaat was not opened. They are not used as evidence.

sections.heading: Trade-offs and consequences
sections.content:
- **Agriculture, long term (risk, not observation).** Solar plants on farmland would take land out of production for the life of the plant. No source gives the area. Illustrative arithmetic from one project only: Khobna is 237 MW on 267.74 ha, about 1.1 ha per MW (SRC-TG-371). The conditional 2030 gap in FND-TG-192 (about 1,350 MW below 3,815 MW and 2,330 MW below 4,800 MW if every listed pipeline project is built) is a calculation, not a forecast. If all of it were utility PV at that density, it would take roughly 1,500-2,600 ha. This mixes wind, rooftop and PV and rests on one site, so it is an order of magnitude only and says nothing on land class.
- **Agriculture and pastoral communities.** The Khobna study says the direct impact zone covers "terres agricoles et pastorales" and that local agriculture is mainly olive, almond and pistachio trees and market gardening (SRC-TG-371). Loss of grazing land is a possible effect on herders; the developer reports no objection from consulted communities.
- **Loss of the legal tool.** Under law 83-87, change of use of farmland goes through a regional commission opinion and a decree or arrêté, which leave a traceable record (FND-TG-841). Art. 5 bis says renewables need no change of use of farmland, so land could be used with no such record (inference from the text). This is why the area affected cannot be counted today.
- **Whole decree-law.** Art. 17 (three-month deadline, Investment Authority fallback) and art. 28 (regularisation of industrial plants built on farmland) weaken farmland protection for other investments. This belongs to FND-TG-841, linked under `creates`.
- **Water and energy.** Not examined beyond the grid-cost rule. Water use by plants is raised by Tozeur farmers in a press piece that could not be read in full, so no water claim is made.

sections.heading: Verdict and gap
sections.content:
**partially-solves.** It removes a legal land obstacle and a grid-cost obstacle for renewables, which are real but secondary causes. No evidence shows faster delivery. At the same time it opens a path to farmland use with no safeguards and no records. It is not counterproductive on the evidence found: the one documented site was grazing land, and the loss to cropland is not shown. Escalating to "counterproductive" would need land-use data that does not exist.

For phase 3: a siting rule (State, degraded or non-productive land first, limits by land class), a public register of land used by solar plants, dual-use criteria built on the ANME agrivoltaics pilot, and fixing the offtaker and grid causes that actually drive the 2030 gap.

sections.heading: Verification
sections.content:
**Independent review, 22 November 2026:** pass after corrections. Originals opened: gazette PDF of decree-law 2022-68 (JORT No. 114, 21 October 2022, arts. 17, 21, 22, 28; SRC-TG-202 url), decree 2016-1123 art. 14 table (SRC-TG-201), the EIB-hosted Khobna ESIA summary (sections 1, 1.2, impact zone, local economy; 237 MW, 267.74 ha, grazing, no objection), the allAfrica/La Presse article of 28 April 2026 (five concessions, farmland, tariff and arbitration remarks), La Presse of 12 September 2025 (ANME demonstrators, GIZ-funded studies), L'Economiste Maghrébin of 29 October 2022; FND-TG-192 for the 1,350-2,330 MW arithmetic. Corrections: art. 17 excludes projects falling under the Investment Authority (added); the 2016 decree, not 2015, and its 10 MW ceiling concerns local-consumption projects (fixed); claims that art. 5 bis removes "the only" land protection or that law 83-87 "does not apply" narrowed to what the text says (it overrides arts. 6 and 8 only); the "d'office" wording is the Juridoc summary's, not the gazette's; the 1,350-2,330 MW gap now stated as conditional; the claim that the measures aim at land and grid problems is marked as the press summary's framing. Scores and verdict unchanged. Not verified in any original: the Khobna 237 MW versus 198 MW difference, hectares of the other concessions, any farmers' union or NGO criticism, and any ANME pilot result; the record states these as unconfirmed.
Teammate sign-off is outstanding. Note for the SRC-TG-202 owner: that record holds no extract of arts. 17, 21, 22, 28 and should get the gazette text.

resolvedSources.title: Énergie renouvelable: nouvelles dispositions pour résoudre les problèmes d'ordre foncier et de raccordement au réseau STEG
resolvedSources.extracts:
Summary of decree-law 2022-68 as reported (29 October 2022):

> sur des parcelles du domaine public agricole et non agricole

> un droit réel spécial est créé sur les bâtiments, ouvrages et équipements

> ne requiert pas, toutefois, de changement de vocation de ces terres

English gloss: renewable projects may be built on public agricultural and non-agricultural plots under lease; a special real right is created over buildings and equipment but not the land; building on agricultural land does not require a change of use of that land.
resolvedSources.notes: Press summary only (tier C). It matches article 21 of the decree-law, which was opened in the gazette PDF (see SRC-TG-202). Extracts are those returned by the page fetch; the page was not read in full.

resolvedSources.title: Centrale solaire photovoltaïque de 237 MW à Khobna (Mazzouna, Sidi Bouzid): résumé non technique de l'étude d'impact environnemental et social
resolvedSources.publisher: Qair Tunisie (developer); study by ASF Consulting; published on the European Investment Bank public register
resolvedSources.extracts:
Section 1 (résumé non technique), project description:

> Le projet comprend la construction d'une centrale photovoltaïque sur une superficie d'environ 267 hectares, la construction d'une ligne aérienne de 225 kV sur une distance de 45 kilomètres

Section 1.2, site:

> sur un terrain appartenant à l'État. D'une superficie de 267,74 hectares, il se trouve à environ 3 kilomètres de Mazzouna et à 5,5 kilomètres de la sabkha de Noual (zone Ramsar). Le site est actuellement utilisé pour le pâturage intensif, sans culture ni aucune activité agricole. Les communautés locales consultées n'ont émis aucune objection à l'affectation de ce site au projet.

Impact zone section:

> Les impacts directs concernent principalement les terres agricoles et pastorales, ainsi que les zones traversées par la ligne.

Section 1.11.2, local economy:

> Agriculture : pilier de l'économie locale, elle emploie plus d'un quart de la population active, avec une prédominance de l'arboriculture (oliviers, amandiers et pistachiers) et du maraîchage.

English gloss: about 267.74 ha of State-owned land currently used for intensive grazing, with no cropping; the developer reports no objection from consulted communities; direct impacts concern mainly farmland and pastureland in the 500 m impact zone; local agriculture is mainly tree crops and market gardening.
resolvedSources.notes: Developer's own consultant document (non-technical summary), so claims about no objection and current land use are the developer's, not independently checked. Capacity is 237 MW here; the 2026 parliamentary report (SRC-TG-372) gives 198 MW for Khobna; not reconciled (could be DC versus AC, or two different projects). Document date not shown in the text read; field measurements are dated 2025. Only the non-technical summary and early sections were searched, not the full 29 pages.

resolvedSources.title: Veille juridique 09-23 : Possibilité de changer la vocation de terres agricoles sur lesquelles ont été implantés des projets industriels avant le 21 octobre 2022
resolvedSources.extracts:
Introduction (public part of the page):

> la procédure applicable au changement de vocation des terres agricoles en vue de réaliser des opérations d'investissement direct au sens de la Loi n° 2016-71 du 30 septembre 2016 portant loi de l'investissement, a été considérablement assouplie depuis 2019.

> -Dans un premier temps (en 2019) : Suite à la modification de la loi n° 83-87 du 11 novembre 1983 relative à la protection des terres agricoles, par la loi n° 2019-47 du 29 mai 2019, relative à l'amélioration du climat de l'investissement, (notamment par l'ajout d'un article 8 ter), le changement de vocation de ces terres n'est plus soumis à l'autorisation du ministre de l'agriculture, mais au seul avis de la commission technique consultative régionale des terres agricoles territorialement compétente. La commission est tenue de répondre à la demande de changement de vocation, dans un délai maximum de trois mois à compter du dépôt de la demande.

> -Dans un deuxième temps (en 2022) : Suite à la modification de l'article 8 ter de la loi n° 83-87 [...] par le décret-loi n° 2022-68 du 19 octobre 2022 [...], l'article 8 ter (nouveau) dispose qu'après l'expiration du délai de 3 mois, le dossier est automatiquement transmis à la Commission des autorisations et des agréments relevant de l'Instance tunisienne de l'investissement, et l'autorisation de changement de vocation, est alors accordée d'office, après que la Commission ait au préalable vérifié si les conditions et les délais requis aient été respectés.

English gloss: since 2019 the procedure to change the use of farmland for direct investment projects has been eased in two steps. In 2019 (law 2019-47, new article 8 ter), the change no longer needs the agriculture minister's authorisation, only the opinion of the regional commission, which must answer within three months. In 2022 (decree-law 2022-68), once the three months expire the file goes automatically to the investment authority's approvals commission and the change is granted automatically ("d'office") after it checks conditions and deadlines.

> les projets industriels ayant été implantés sur des terres à vocation agricole avant le 21 octobre 2022, sans changement de vocation préalable sont considérés comme des projets industriels implantés illégalement. Cependant [...] certains terrains à vocation agricole sur lesquels ont été implantés des projets industriels avant le 21 octobre, pourraient, a postériori, faire l'objet d'un changement de vocation, et ce en application de l'article 28 du décret-loi n° 2022-68 du 19 octobre 2022 [...]. Ces critères et conditions viennent d'être fixés par l'arrêté de la ministre de l'industrie du 3 mai 2023

> - La capacité d'employabilité du projet ne soit pas inférieure à 50 emplois ; [...] - La surface fonctionnelle du projet ne soit pas inférieure à 1500 m2 ;

English gloss: industrial projects built on farmland before 21 October 2022 without a change of vocation are illegal, but some can be regularised after the fact under article 28 of decree-law 2022-68, under criteria set by the industry minister's order of 3 May 2023 (including at least 50 jobs and at least 1,500 m2 of functional area).
resolvedSources.notes: Commentary by a commercial legal database, not the gazette text; the texts of law 2019-47, decree-law 2022-68 and the arrêté of 3 May 2023 were not opened. That law 83-87 was amended by 2019-47 and by decree-law 2022-68 is confirmed by gazette visas (SRC-TG-843, SRC-TG-844). The rest of the page is behind a paywall.
